subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 a person is guilty of the offence of money laundering where he-

options.A: holds property abroad without the permission of the Reserve Bank of India, whatever the source from which it was acquired
options.B: receives cash in excess of the prescribed limit in a single transaction, whether or not the money has any criminal origin
options.C: is knowingly a party to, or actually involved in, any process or activity connected with the proceeds of crime and projects it as untainted property
options.D: earns income from a lawful business and fails to disclose the whole of that income in the return filed by him for the year

answer_html:
Answer: (C) is knowingly a party to, or actually involved in, any process or activity connected with the proceeds of crime and projects it as untainted property.

The offence covers any process or activity by a person which directly or indirectly attempts to indulge, or knowingly assists, or of which he is knowingly a party or is actually involved, connected with the proceeds of crime including its concealment, possession, acquisition or use, and projecting or claiming it as untainted property. Money laundering is the processing of criminal proceeds so as to disguise their illegal origin, converting the dirty money so that it appears to be legitimate money.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The stage at which the money launderer first introduces the illegal funds into the financial system, often by breaking a large amount of cash into smaller and less conspicuous sums deposited into a bank account, is-
answer_html:
Answer: (A) placement.

At the placement stage the launderer introduces the illegal funds into the financial system, typically by breaking up a large amount of cash into less conspicuous smaller sums deposited directly into a bank account, or by using instruments such as cheques and bank drafts. Layering is the series of continuous conversions or movements of funds which hides their true origin and distances them from their criminal source. Integration is the stage at which the funds reach the legitimate economy and become inseparably mixed with money earned from lawful sources.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The central national agency responsible for receiving, processing, analysing and disseminating information relating to suspect financial transactions is-
answer_html:
Answer: (C) the Financial Intelligence Unit - India.

The Financial Intelligence Unit - India, under the Department of Revenue in the Ministry of Finance, is the central national agency responsible for receiving, processing, analysing and disseminating information relating to suspect financial transactions to enforcement agencies and to foreign Financial Intelligence Units. It was set up in November 2004, is headed by a Director in the rank of Joint Secretary to the Government of India, and reports directly to the Economic Intelligence Council headed by the Finance Minister.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002-

options.A: was enacted in January 2003 and came into force, along with the Rules made under it, with effect from 1 July 2005
options.B: was enacted in January 2003 and came into force, along with the Rules made under it, with effect from 1 April 2003
options.C: was enacted in July 2005 and came into force, along with the Rules made under it, with effect from 1 January 2006
options.D: was enacted in January 2003 but the Rules made under it were brought into force only with effect from 2013

answer_html:
Answer: (A) was enacted in January 2003 and came into force, along with the Rules made under it, with effect from 1 July 2005.

The Act was enacted in January 2003, and the Act along with the Rules framed under it came into force with effect from 1 July 2005. It extends to the whole of India. It was amended by the Prevention of Money Laundering (Amendment) Act 2009 with effect from 1 June 2009, and further amended by the Prevention of Money Laundering (Amendment) Act, 2012 with effect from 15 February 2013.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 consists of-

options.A: ten chapters containing seventy-five sections, together with one Schedule
options.B: five chapters containing seventy-five sections, together with two Schedules
options.C: ten chapters containing fifty-seven sections, together with three Schedules
options.D: twelve chapters containing ninety-five sections, together with one Schedule

answer_html:
Answer: (A) ten chapters containing seventy-five sections, together with one Schedule.

The Act consists of ten chapters containing 75 sections and one Schedule. Chapter I contains sections 1 and 2 dealing with the short title, extent and commencement and the definitions; Chapter II contains sections 3 and 4 providing for the offence of money laundering and its punishment; Chapter III, sections 5 to 11, provides for attachment, adjudication and confiscation; Chapter IV, sections 12 to 15, deals with the obligations of banking companies, financial institutions and intermediaries; and Chapter V, sections 16 to 24, relates to summons, searches and seizures.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The offences listed in the Schedule to the Act are divided into-

options.A: two parts, Part A listing offences under the Indian Penal Code and Part B covering every other scheduled offence whatever its value may be
options.B: five parts, of which only the first covers offences of a total value of ₹1 crore or more, the remaining four dealing with trans-border crimes
options.C: three parts, Part A listing offences in 28 paragraphs, Part B covering offences of a total value of ₹1 crore or more, and Part C trans-border crimes
options.D: three parts, Part A covering offences of a total value of ₹1 crore or more, Part B trans-border crimes, and Part C offences under the Indian Penal Code

answer_html:
Answer: (C) three parts, Part A listing offences in 28 paragraphs, Part B covering offences of a total value of ₹1 crore or more, and Part C trans-border crimes.

The scheduled offences are divided into three parts. Part A lists offences in 28 paragraphs, drawn from statutes such as the Indian Penal Code, the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances legislation, the Explosive Substances Act, 1908, the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, the Arms Act, 1959, the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. Part B covers offences where the total value involved is ₹1 crore or more. Part C deals with trans-border crimes.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The proposition that every scheduled offence is a predicate offence means that-

options.A: a person convicted of a scheduled offence is automatically taken to have committed the offence of money laundering as well
options.B: the scheduled offence and the offence of money laundering must always be tried together before the same Special Court
options.C: an investigation into a scheduled offence may be initiated only after the money laundering investigation has concluded
options.D: the occurrence of the scheduled offence is a pre-requisite for initiating an investigation into the offence of money laundering

answer_html:
Answer: (D) the occurrence of the scheduled offence is a pre-requisite for initiating an investigation into the offence of money laundering.

Every scheduled offence is a predicate offence, and the occurrence of the scheduled offence is a pre-requisite for initiating an investigation into the offence of money laundering. Conviction for the scheduled offence is not automatically a conviction for money laundering; the two remain distinct offences, the second turning on dealing with the proceeds of the first.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Investigation and prosecution of cases under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act is entrusted to-

options.A: the Adjudicating Authority, which is under the administrative control of the Ministry of Law and Justice
options.B: the Directorate of Enforcement, which is under the administrative control of the Department of Revenue for operational purposes
options.C: the Financial Intelligence Unit - India, which is under the administrative control of the Economic Intelligence Council
options.D: the Central Bureau of Investigation, which is under the administrative control of the Ministry of Home Affairs

answer_html:
Answer: (B) the Directorate of Enforcement, which is under the administrative control of the Department of Revenue for operational purposes.

The Directorate of Enforcement in the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance is responsible for investigating cases of the offence of money laundering, and the work relating to investigation and prosecution of cases under the Act has been entrusted to it. The Directorate is under the administrative control of the Department of Revenue for operational purposes, and it is also responsible for the enforcement of the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999. The Financial Intelligence Unit gathers and disseminates information; it does not prosecute.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Under the Act, the Adjudicating Authority and the Appellate Tribunal have been constituted respectively under-

options.A: Section 8 and Section 43, the Tribunal hearing appeals against the orders of the designated Special Court
options.B: Section 6 and Section 25, the Tribunal hearing appeals against the orders of the Adjudicating Authority
options.C: Section 25 and Section 6, the Tribunal hearing appeals against the orders of the Adjudicating Authority
options.D: Section 5 and Section 12, the Tribunal hearing appeals only against orders of confiscation of property

answer_html:
Answer: (B) Section 6 and Section 25, the Tribunal hearing appeals against the orders of the Adjudicating Authority.

The Adjudicating Authority is constituted in terms of Section 6 of the Act and is appointed by the Central Government; its function is essentially to confirm attachment or to order confiscation of attached properties. Where it decides that any property is involved in money laundering it confirms, by an order in writing, the attachment of the property or the retention of the property or records seized. The Appellate Tribunal established under Section 25 hears appeals against the orders of the Adjudicating Authority and of the authorities under the Act, including the Director of the Financial Intelligence Unit.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The Appellate Tribunal established under Section 25 of the Act consists of-

options.A: a Chairperson and six other Members
options.B: a Chairperson and two other Members
options.C: a Chairperson and four other Members
options.D: a Chairperson and one other Member

answer_html:
Answer: (B) a Chairperson and two other Members.

The Tribunal consists of a Chairperson and two other Members. The Act also allows a Chairperson or Member holding such a post in any other Tribunal established under any law for the time being in force to be appointed as the Chairperson or a Member of the Appellate Tribunal under this Act.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: A person guilty of the offence of money laundering is punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term-

options.A: of not less than seven years, which may extend to ten years, but is not liable to fine
options.B: of not less than five years, which may extend to seven years, but is not liable to fine
options.C: of not less than three years, which may extend to seven years, and is also liable to fine
options.D: of not less than one year, which may extend to three years, and is also liable to fine

answer_html:
Answer: (C) of not less than three years, which may extend to seven years, and is also liable to fine.

The offence is punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than three years but which may extend to seven years, and the offender is also liable to fine. Where the proceeds of crime involved relate to an offence specified under paragraph 2 of Part A of the Schedule, the maximum punishment may extend to ten years instead of seven.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: For the trial of an offence punishable under Section 4 of the Act, a Special Court is designated-

options.A: by the Central Government in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court, from among the Courts of Session
options.B: by the State Government in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court, from among the Courts of Session
options.C: by the Central Government on the recommendation of the Adjudicating Authority, from among the Metropolitan Magistrates
options.D: by the High Court itself on the application of the Directorate of Enforcement, from among the Courts of Judicial Magistrates

answer_html:
Answer: (A) by the Central Government in consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court, from among the Courts of Session.

The Central Government, in consultation with the Chief Justice of the respective High Court, designates by notification one or more Courts of Session as a Special Court for such area or areas or for such case or class or group of cases as may be specified. The Special Court also tries the offences with which the accused may, under the Code of Criminal Procedure, be charged at the same trial. An offence of money laundering and any connected scheduled offence are triable by the Special Court constituted for the area in which the offence has been committed.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Among the obligations cast on a reporting entity by Section 12 of the Act is the obligation to maintain the record of documents evidencing the identity of its clients and beneficial owners, and the account files, for a period of-

options.A: three years after the business relationship has ended or the account has been closed, whichever is later
options.B: ten years after the business relationship has ended or the account has been closed, whichever is later
options.C: eight years after the business relationship has ended or the account has been closed, whichever is later
options.D: five years after the business relationship has ended or the account has been closed, whichever is later

answer_html:
Answer: (D) five years after the business relationship has ended or the account has been closed, whichever is later.

Section 12 requires every reporting entity to maintain a record of all prescribed transactions in a manner enabling it to reconstruct individual transactions, to furnish information about such transactions to the Director of the Financial Intelligence Unit within the prescribed time, to verify the identity of its clients, to identify the beneficial owner where there is one, and to maintain records of identity documents and account files for five years after the business relationship has ended or the account has been closed, whichever is later. A reporting entity means a banking company, financial institution, intermediary or a person carrying on a designated business or profession.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: A transaction is a suspicious transaction where, to a person acting in good faith, it-

options.A: is carried out with a counterparty situated in a jurisdiction which has not entered into a bilateral agreement with India under the Act
options.B: gives rise to a reasonable ground of suspicion that it may involve the proceeds of crime, or appears to have no economic rationale or bona fide purpose
options.C: is made in cash and exceeds the monetary threshold prescribed for the recording of cash transactions by a reporting entity in any month
options.D: is carried out by a client whose identity has not been verified in the manner and subject to the conditions prescribed by the Rules

answer_html:
Answer: (B) gives rise to a reasonable ground of suspicion that it may involve the proceeds of crime, or appears to have no economic rationale or bona fide purpose.

A suspicious transaction is one which, to a person acting in good faith, gives rise to a reasonable ground of suspicion that it may involve the proceeds of crime, or appears to have been made in circumstances of unusual or unjustified complexity, or appears to have no economic rationale or bona fide purpose. Every banking company must furnish details of suspicious transactions whether or not they are made in cash, so the fact that a transaction is not in cash, and the fact that it falls below a cash threshold, are both immaterial.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
case_facts_html:
Kaveri Cooperative Bank Limited is a banking company and therefore a reporting entity under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 and the Rules made under it.

During the month of May 2026 the following transactions pass through its books:

(i) a single cash deposit of ₹14 lakh made by a trading concern into its current account;

(ii) a cross border wire transfer of ₹6 lakh, the destination of the funds being in India;

(iii) the registration by the bank of a purchase of immovable property valued at ₹55 lakh;

(iv) a cash transaction of ₹40,000 in which a counterfeit currency note is tendered as genuine;

(v) the opening on 4 May 2026 of an account for a new client whose identity has been verified.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. As regards transaction (iv), the cash transaction of ₹40,000 in which a counterfeit note is tendered, the bank-

options.A: must record it, transactions with counterfeit currency being recordable without any monetary threshold
options.B: need not record it, the amount involved being far below the threshold of ₹10 lakh for cash transactions
options.C: need not record it, a transaction becoming recordable only where the counterfeiting is admitted by the client
options.D: must record it, but only if the aggregate of such transactions in the month exceeds ₹10 lakh in value

answer_html:
Answer: (A) must record it, transactions with counterfeit currency being recordable without any monetary threshold.

Every reporting entity must maintain a record of all transactions with counterfeit currency. No monetary threshold is attached to that limb, so the amount of ₹40,000 is immaterial. The threshold of ₹10 lakh governs the separate limbs dealing with cash transactions and with receipts, not the counterfeit currency limb.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
case_facts_html:
Kaveri Cooperative Bank Limited is a banking company and therefore a reporting entity under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 and the Rules made under it.

During the month of May 2026 the following transactions pass through its books:

(i) a single cash deposit of ₹14 lakh made by a trading concern into its current account;

(ii) a cross border wire transfer of ₹6 lakh, the destination of the funds being in India;

(iii) the registration by the bank of a purchase of immovable property valued at ₹55 lakh;

(iv) a cash transaction of ₹40,000 in which a counterfeit currency note is tendered as genuine;

(v) the opening on 4 May 2026 of an account for a new client whose identity has been verified.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. As regards transaction (ii), the cross border wire transfer of ₹6 lakh, the bank-

options.A: need not record it, the threshold for a cross border wire transfer being a value of more than ₹10 lakh
options.B: need not record it, because the destination of the funds rather than their origin is situated in India
options.C: must record it only if the transfer is made in cash, a wire transfer otherwise falling outside the Rules
options.D: must record it, the threshold for a cross border wire transfer being a value of more than ₹5 lakh

answer_html:
Answer: (D) must record it, the threshold for a cross border wire transfer being a value of more than ₹5 lakh.

A reporting entity must record all cross border wire transfers of a value of more than ₹5 lakh or its equivalent in foreign currency where either the origin or the destination of the funds is in India. The transfer of ₹6 lakh exceeds that threshold, and it is enough that the destination is in India.

(i) a single cash deposit of ₹14 lakh made by a trading concern into its current account;

(iii) the registration by the bank of a purchase of immovable property valued at ₹55 lakh;

(iv) a cash transaction of ₹40,000 in which a counterfeit currency note is tendered as genuine;

(v) the opening on 4 May 2026 of an account for a new client whose identity has been verified.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. As regards transaction (iii), the purchase of immovable property valued at ₹55 lakh registered by the bank, the record-keeping obligation-

options.A: does not arise, the threshold for a purchase or sale of immovable property being a value of ₹1 crore or more
options.B: does not arise, because the obligation extends only to transactions in cash and not to registered transfers
options.C: arises, but only in respect of a sale of immovable property and not in respect of a purchase of property
options.D: arises, the threshold for a purchase or sale of immovable property being a value of ₹50 lakh or more

answer_html:
Answer: (D) arises, the threshold for a purchase or sale of immovable property being a value of ₹50 lakh or more.

Every reporting entity must maintain a record of all purchases and sales by any person of immovable property valued at fifty lakh rupees or more which is registered by the reporting entity. The value of ₹55 lakh crosses that threshold, and the limb applies to a purchase as much as to a sale.

(i) a single cash deposit of ₹14 lakh made by a trading concern into its current account;

(iii) the registration by the bank of a purchase of immovable property valued at ₹55 lakh;

(v) the opening on 4 May 2026 of an account for a new client whose identity has been verified.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. The principal officer of Kaveri Cooperative Bank Limited must furnish the information relating to the reportable transactions of May 2026 to the Director-

options.A: by 15 May 2027, the information being furnished once a year by the 15th of the succeeding May
options.B: by 30 June 2026, the information being furnished every month by the 30th of the succeeding month
options.C: by 15 June 2026, the information being furnished every month by the 15th of the succeeding month
options.D: by 31 May 2026, the information being furnished every month by the last day of that same month

answer_html:
Answer: (C) by 15 June 2026, the information being furnished every month by the 15th of the succeeding month.

Every reporting entity must designate a principal officer, who reports to the Director of the Financial Intelligence Unit. The principal officer must furnish the information relating to the reportable transactions to the Director every month by the 15th of the succeeding month, so the transactions of May 2026 must be reported by 15 June 2026. Separately, the entity must file the electronic KYC data with the Central KYC Records Registry within 10 days.
